questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Diagnostic body structures distinguish five higher nonchordate groups without relying on names alone
questions.syllabus_anchor: Animal Kingdom: Arthropoda; Mollusca; Echinodermata; Hemichordata
questions.question: A classification key lists P with jointed appendages and an exoskeleton, Q with a mantle and muscular foot, R with an adult water-vascular system and pentaradial body plan, and S with proboscis, collar and trunk. Which ordered assignment fits?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata.
Why: Jointed appendages and an exoskeleton identify the arthropod combination. A mantle and muscular foot distinguish the molluscan plan. The water-vascular system, considered with adult pentaradial organisation, supports Echinodermata. The three-region body of proboscis, collar and trunk is characteristic of hemichordates; it must not be replaced by a chordate identity merely because of the historical name. Each assignment uses a distinctive structure rather than a general feature such as having a body cavity.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges arthropod and annelid characters and misassigns the last two groups. (B) gives a mantle-bearing animal an annelid identity and misclassifies S. (C) ignores the echinoderm water-vascular system.
Key point: Use diagnostic combinations to navigate a classification key.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.sub_topic: A selective wall defect separates collenchymatous support from lignified fibres and vessels
questions.syllabus_anchor: Anatomy of Flowering Plants: tissue systems; collenchyma; sclerenchyma; xylem
questions.question: The tissue diagram labels P as living elongated cells with uneven corner thickening, Q as dead heavily lignified fibres with narrow lumens, and R as a perforated conducting tube in a vascular bundle. A defect prevents normal lignification but leaves the corner-thickening process intact. Which prediction best distinguishes the tissue effects?
options: A) All three must become identical parenchyma immediately
B) P can retain collenchymatous support, while Q support and R's resistance to collapse are compromised
C) P loses all walls, while Q and R are unchanged because they are dead
D) R becomes phloem solely because its walls contain less lignin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Collenchyma and lignified support/conducting elements depend on different wall features.
Why: P's living cells and uneven corner thickening identify collenchyma, whose support does not depend on the same heavily lignified wall pattern as sclerenchymatous Q. R's perforated tube is a xylem vessel element arrangement; lignified walls help it withstand mechanical stresses and resist collapse during water transport. Being dead at maturity does not make Q and R independent of the wall properties established during differentiation. The specified defect therefore affects the tissues differently.
Why not the others: (A) assumes an immediate cell-identity conversion not caused by the stated defect. (C) destroys the explicitly preserved thickening mechanism and ignores lignified walls in dead mature cells. (D) treats loss of one wall component as automatic conversion between vascular tissues.
Key point: Link wall composition to function without replacing tissue identity.
questions.image_alt: P has thick corners; Q has thick narrow-lumen walls; R is a perforated conducting tube in vascular tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Meiotic pairing and exchange ordered separately from the two segregation events
questions.syllabus_anchor: Cell Cycle and Cell Division: meiosis I and II; synapsis; crossing over
questions.question: Four meiotic events are recorded: homologous chromosomes pair, nonsister chromatids exchange corresponding segments, homologues separate while sister centromeres remain joined, and sister chromatids separate. Which ordering and interpretation are correct?
options: A) Synapsis precedes crossing over; homologues separate in division I and sisters in division II
B) Crossing over precedes synapsis; sister chromatids separate in division I
C) Homologues and sister chromatids always separate together in the first division
D) All four events are ordinary metaphase events of mitosis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pairing precedes crossing over, followed by the two different segregation events.
Why: Homologous pairing develops during zygotene, and crossing over between nonsister chromatids occurs during pachytene of prophase I. At anaphase I the homologous chromosomes move apart without the sister centromeres dividing in the ordinary meiotic pattern. Sister chromatids are separated during the second meiotic division. The chromosome relationships therefore differ at the two anaphases even though both move genetic material toward opposite poles.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the pairing/exchange sequence and assigns the wrong segregation event to division I. (C) eliminates the defining distinction between the two divisions. (D) assigns homologous synapsis and crossing over to ordinary mitosis.
Key point: Track homologues and sisters as different chromosome relationships.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: A blocked return intermediate distinguishes transient C4 decarboxylation from sustained acceptor regeneration
questions.syllabus_anchor: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants: the C4 pathway; cellular compartmentation
questions.question: In a C4 leaf, a four-carbon acid normally moves from mesophyll to bundle-sheath cells, releases CO2 there, and leaves a three-carbon compound that returns for acceptor regeneration. A selective block prevents this return while initially leaving decarboxylation and RuBisCO intact. Which early-to-later effect is most consistent?
options: A) Calvin-cycle reactions must all relocate into mesophyll cells
B) The initial four-carbon acid directly becomes RuBisCO and replaces its gene
C) Some existing acid can still release CO2, but sustained PEP regeneration and the concentrating shuttle decline
D) The block proves that C4 plants never use ATP for acceptor regeneration
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Existing intermediates can support a transient step, but the carbon shuttle cannot be sustained.
Why: The initial carbon acceptor in the mesophyll is PEP. Its regeneration uses the returning three-carbon intermediate and requires energy. Existing four-carbon acid can initially reach a functioning decarboxylation step, so a transport block need not instantly poison RuBisCO or erase every intermediate. Over time, failure to return and regenerate the acceptor restricts continued operation of the concentrating pathway. The Calvin cycle remains associated with bundle-sheath CO2 fixation in the stated C4 arrangement.
Why not the others: (A) invents relocation of the Calvin cycle as an automatic response. (B) confuses a metabolic intermediate with a protein. (D) reverses the energetic requirement of PEP regeneration.
Key point: Separate a transient use of existing intermediates from a pathway's sustained regeneration requirement.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Preserved thyroxine feedback does not exclude loss of parathyroid calcium regulation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Chemical Coordination and Integration: parathyroid hormone; thyroid calcitonin; endocrine functions
questions.question: In a limited endocrine model, parathyroid output is lost while thyroid thyroxine production and its pituitary feedback remain normal. Blood calcium falls and neuromuscular excitability rises. Which interpretation follows without treating all thyroid-region hormones as one signal?
options: A) Normal thyroxine proves that parathyroid hormone is also normal
B) Calcitonin deficiency is the stated cause, and PTH would lower calcium further
C) TSH directly supplies all missing calcium to the circulation
D) Loss of calcium-raising PTH fits the model; thyroid calcitonin has an opposing calcium-related action distinct from thyroxine
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) PTH and calcitonin act in calcium regulation, whereas normal thyroxine does not replace PTH.
Why: Parathyroid hormone is a calcium-raising hormone, and its loss can account for the stipulated low-calcium effect in this model. Thyroid calcitonin has an opposing influence on blood calcium, but it is not the same substance as thyroid hormone involved in metabolic regulation. Normal thyroxine and its feedback therefore cannot be used as a test of intact parathyroid output. The question fixes the lesion and asks for hormonal interpretation rather than a unique diagnosis from symptoms alone.
Why not the others: (A) treats anatomically nearby endocrine sources as functionally identical. (B) reverses the calcium effect of PTH and changes the stipulated lesion. (C) assigns direct calcium supply to a pituitary signal.
Key point: Identify each hormone's source and regulated variable separately.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Three stage-and-site constraints distinguish later embryo transfer, GIFT and ICSI
questions.syllabus_anchor: Reproductive Health: infertility; assisted reproductive technologies
questions.question: Three assisted-reproduction plans are considered. P has a four-cell laboratory embryo but both oviducts are blocked and the uterus can support transfer. Q requires a donor ovum and has a patent oviduct; fertilisation is intended to occur inside her body. R requires a sperm to be injected directly into an oocyte. Which complete plan fits the stated stages and sites?
options: A) P culture beyond eight blastomeres then intrauterine transfer; Q GIFT; R ICSI
B) P transfer the four-cell embryo into a blocked tube; Q GIFT; R ICSI
C) P culture then intrauterine transfer; Q transfer an already fertilised embryo as the unfertilised donor ovum; R ICSI
D) P culture then intrauterine transfer; Q GIFT; R insemination into the uterus instead of the oocyte
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Further culture with intrauterine transfer, GIFT and ICSI match the three constraints.
Step 1: Early embryos up to eight blastomeres can normally be transferred to the tube, but P's blocked tubes invalidate that route. Further culture permits transfer of a later embryo to the functional uterus.
Step 2: Q's aim is fertilisation within her body using a donor ovum. Gamete intrafallopian transfer provides the appropriate unfertilised gamete and patent-tube site.
Step 3: Direct sperm injection into the oocyte is intracytoplasmic sperm injection, a different operation from placing semen in the reproductive tract.
Why: Embryonic stage, anatomical access and whether fertilisation has already happened all constrain the route.
Why not the others: (B) ignores the tubal obstruction. (C) substitutes an embryo for the required unfertilised ovum. (D) confuses an intrauterine insemination site with the oocyte cytoplasm.
Key point: Match reproductive technology to stage, site and biological purpose.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: A deliberately mischarged adaptor separates amino-acid specificity from codon decoding
questions.syllabus_anchor: Molecular Basis of Inheritance: translation; tRNA; amino-acid activation
questions.question: In a supplied cell-free translation experiment, a tRNA with anticodon 3-prime UUU 5-prime is artificially charged with valine instead of its usual lysine. Editing is bypassed, and the ribosome accepts it at mRNA codon 5-prime AAA 3-prime. What does this event demonstrate?
options: A) The AAA bases must have changed into a valine codon
B) The anticodon can select the AAA position while incorrect charging supplies valine there
C) The ribosome necessarily converts the attached valine chemically into lysine
D) Amino-acid charging and codon recognition are the same molecular recognition event
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Codon placement and amino-acid attachment are distinct specificity steps.
Why: The anticodon pairs antiparallel with the AAA codon, directing where this tRNA is used. The amino acid delivered is the molecule actually attached to the adaptor, here stipulated to be valine after editing has been bypassed. Normally aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase recognition and associated checks help maintain the correct amino-acid assignment. This experiment separates that charging specificity from the codon–anticodon interaction rather than changing the genetic code or the mRNA sequence.
Why not the others: (A) invents an RNA sequence mutation. (C) assigns amino-acid conversion to the ribosome without any such reaction. (D) ignores that different sites and recognition processes determine charging and decoding.
Key point: An adaptor's anticodon and its attached amino acid convey different information.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Dose-response adaptation separated from withdrawal and plant-source classification
questions.syllabus_anchor: Human Health and Disease: drugs and alcohol abuse; tolerance; dependence
questions.question: Report P describes needing increasing doses of an opioid to obtain a formerly achieved effect. Report Q describes withdrawal symptoms when repeated use is stopped. A third report identifies cocaine as a stimulant despite its plant origin. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) P and Q both mean that a protective immune response has developed
B) P proves physical dependence, while Q establishes only a higher dose requirement
C) Plant origin makes cocaine and all opioids identical receptor agonists
D) P describes tolerance, Q supports dependence, and plant origin alone does not determine drug class or action
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Tolerance, dependence and pharmacological class must be distinguished.
Why: Tolerance refers to reduced response to a previously effective dose, so the required dose may rise. Dependence is supported by a withdrawal syndrome after discontinuation in the stated history. These phenomena can coexist but are not interchangeable definitions. Drug source is another independent property: cocaine's plant origin does not make its stimulant action or molecular targets identical to opioid actions. The reports therefore describe different dimensions of drug use.
Why not the others: (A) confuses nervous-system adaptation with immunity to infection. (B) exchanges the two operational observations. (C) classifies receptor action from source alone and contradicts the stimulant description.
Key point: Classify the measured effect rather than treating every repeated-use change as dependence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Transgenic protein production separated from resource-provenance and biopiracy concerns
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biotechnology and Its Applications: transgenic animals; ethical issues
questions.question: A transgenic animal expresses a human therapeutic protein in milk, followed by product purification. Separately, a company uses a community's biological resource and documented traditional knowledge without proper authorisation or benefit sharing. Which distinction is appropriate?
options: A) Successful transgene expression by itself proves that every related patent claim is justified
B) Purification of a therapeutic protein is the definition of biopiracy
C) The first is a transgenic production application; the second raises biopiracy concerns, and expression alone does not settle provenance or ethical permission
D) Traditional knowledge can never be relevant to the use of a biological resource
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Technical production and the ethical provenance of resource use are different questions.
Why: Transgenic animals can be used to produce biologically useful human proteins; recovery and purification are then required to obtain a usable product. Biopiracy concerns unauthorised or unfair commercial use of biological resources and associated knowledge, as stipulated in the separate case. Demonstrating that a gene can be expressed does not establish the origin of the resource, consent or fair sharing. The question distinguishes biological application from the ethical issue rather than deciding the validity of a particular real patent.
Why not the others: (A) substitutes technical success for an assessment of provenance and permission. (B) misdefines a processing step as resource appropriation. (D) dismisses the very knowledge specified as part of the resource use.
Key point: Separate what a technology does from how its inputs and knowledge were obtained.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Four biodiversity-loss drivers identified by their distinct causal observations
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biodiversity and Conservation: habitat loss; alien species; overexploitation; co-extinction
questions.question: Four biodiversity losses are observed: a forest is divided into isolated patches; an introduced predator eliminates native island prey; a commercially harvested species declines under excessive collection; and an obligately pollinated plant disappears after its sole pollinator is lost. Which sequence best identifies the main drivers?
options: B) Habitat fragmentation, invasion, overexploitation, co-extinction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The four observations correspond to fragmentation, invasion, overexploitation and co-extinction.
Why: Dividing habitat reduces continuity and can isolate populations even where some habitat remains. An introduced predator adds an invasive biotic pressure. Excessive removal directly exceeds the harvested population's capacity to persist. In the final case, loss of an indispensable interacting species causes a dependent species to disappear, which is co-extinction. These drivers can interact in real ecosystems, but the observations specify the principal causal change for each case.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges the first two and last two mechanisms. (C) treats collection and introduction as though they were the same process. (D) attributes dependence-related loss to a case where habitat division is the specified cause and misassigns the other observations.
Key point: Identify the causal change, not only the shared outcome of population loss.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Male-only gene flow separates adult allele pooling from sex-specific gamete contributions
questions.syllabus_anchor: Evolution: gene flow; Hardy–Weinberg principle
questions.question: A large recipient population has 200 males and 200 females, with genotype frequencies AA=0.40,Aa=0.20,aa=0.40 separately in each sex. It receives 100 male immigrants with frequencies AA=0.64,Aa=0.32,aa=0.04. Each male contributes equally to the sperm pool and each female equally to the egg pool; mating is random between these pools. What are the pooled adult A-allele frequency and expected heterozygote frequency in the next generation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Adult pooled A frequency is 0.56, while offspring heterozygosity is 0.50.
Given: Migration is male-only and gametic contributions are equal within each sex, not across all adults regardless of sex.
Formula/Principle: Count adult alleles separately from the sperm and egg frequencies used to form offspring.
Step 1: Resident and immigrant A frequencies are \[p_R=0.40+0.20/2=0.50,\quad p_I=0.64+0.32/2=0.80.\] Adult pooling gives \[p_{adult}=\frac{400(0.50)+100(0.80)}{500}=0.56.\]
Step 2: Sperm frequency is \[p_s=\frac{200(0.50)+100(0.80)}{300}=0.60,\] while egg frequency remains pe=0.50.
Step 3: Heterozygotes arise from A sperm with a egg or a sperm with A egg. \[f_{Aa}=p_s(1-p_e)+(1-p_s)p_e=0.60(0.50)+0.40(0.50)=0.50.\]
Why: Male-only immigration makes the two parental allele pools different. Applying 2p(1-p) to the pooled adult p would ignore the stated sex-specific gametic contributions. No founder bottleneck is required.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the immigrant effect on the adult allele count. (B) uses only immigrant frequencies. (C) treats the immigrant AA genotype frequency as an allele-pool quantity and applies the wrong mating model.
Key point: Construct the gamete pools actually used in mating before predicting offspring frequencies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Abiotic organic synthesis distinguished from demonstrated cellular life
questions.syllabus_anchor: Evolution: origin of life; chemical evolution experiments
questions.question: An origin-of-life model circulates a reducing gas mixture through water vapour and electrical discharges in a closed apparatus. Organic compounds, including amino acids, accumulate, but no self-maintaining reproducing cells are detected. What is the strongest warranted conclusion?
options: A) The apparatus has demonstrated the complete origin of a living cell
B) Every modern atmospheric composition must produce the same products
C) Abiotic synthesis of some organic building blocks is possible under the tested conditions; the origin of a living cell has not thereby been demonstrated
D) The organic products prove that electrical energy cannot drive chemical change
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The result demonstrates a chemical-synthesis possibility within its specified conditions.
Why: The model tests whether supplied nonliving starting materials and an energy source can yield organic molecules. Detecting amino acids supports that stage of chemical evolution. A self-maintaining, reproducing cellular system would require additional organisation and processes that the observation explicitly does not establish. The result also depends on the chosen gas mixture and apparatus, so it cannot be transferred without qualification to every atmospheric composition.
Why not the others: (A) equates building blocks with an autonomous living system. (B) ignores the experimental conditions as part of the conclusion. (D) contradicts organic synthesis occurring with electrical discharges.
Key point: Match a claim about life's origin to the level of organisation actually produced.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Quiet breathing linked through diaphragm motion, thoracic volume and pressure gradient
questions.syllabus_anchor: Breathing and Exchange of Gases: mechanism of breathing
questions.question: During quiet inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and thoracic volume increases. Which pressure change draws air inward, and what normally happens during the following quiet expiration?
options: A) Alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric pressure; relaxation reduces thoracic volume and raises alveolar pressure slightly above atmosphere
B) Alveolar pressure rises above atmosphere during inspiration; further diaphragm contraction drives expiration
C) Atmospheric pressure must fall to zero; expiration then needs no pressure difference
D) Both phases require alveolar pressure to remain exactly equal to atmosphere throughout airflow
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A changing alveolar–atmospheric pressure difference directs airflow.
Why: Expansion of the thorax and lungs lowers alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure, allowing air to enter. During ordinary quiet expiration, relaxation and elastic recoil reduce lung volume and raise alveolar pressure slightly above atmosphere, driving air out. The diaphragm's movement changes the volume; it does not directly pull individual air molecules through the airways. At the transition between phases pressures can equalise, but sustained flow requires a pressure gradient.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the inspiratory gradient and the normal diaphragm action in quiet expiration. (C) invents an extreme external pressure change. (D) eliminates the driving gradient while asserting flow.
Key point: Connect muscle action to volume, then pressure, then airflow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: RNA sugar identity and phosphodiester polarity jointly locate the chain-extension site
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biomolecules: nucleic acids; Molecular Basis of Inheritance: transcription; nucleotide polarity
questions.question: The nucleotide diagram shows a strand with a free 5-prime phosphate at the left, 3-prime-to-5-prime phosphodiester connections, and a free 3-prime OH at the right. The illustrated sugars have a 2-prime OH and one base is uracil. Which assignment and chain-extension site follow?
options: A) DNA; add the next nucleotide to the left 5-prime phosphate
B) RNA; add the next nucleotide to a base's amino group
C) RNA; add the next nucleotide to the right 3-prime OH
D) DNA; add the next nucleotide to the right 2-prime OH
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The structure is RNA, and normal chain extension uses the right-hand 3-prime OH.
Why: Ribose has the 2-prime hydroxyl shown, in contrast to deoxyribose's hydrogen at that position. Uracil provides a second compatible RNA feature. The backbone links a sugar's 3-prime position through phosphate to the next sugar's 5-prime position. A new nucleotide is therefore joined at the exposed 3-prime OH, extending the strand in the 5-prime-to-3-prime direction. Base amino groups do not provide the normal backbone extension site.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the sugar and base evidence and extends the wrong end. (B) has the right nucleic-acid identity but an incorrect bonding site. (D) misidentifies the sugar and confuses the diagnostic 2-prime OH with the elongation 3-prime OH.
Key point: Use sugar composition to identify the strand and backbone polarity to locate its growth end.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Upstream oxygenation and downstream recovery separately limit scaled recombinant-product yield
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biotechnology—Principles and Processes: bioreactors; downstream processing
questions.question: Two engineered cultures express the same target protein per viable cell in a small aerated flask. On scale-up, vessel P has poor oxygen transfer and falling viable-cell density. Vessel Q maintains aeration but loses much target during separation and purification. Which distinction best explains why equal small-flask expression does not guarantee equal final product yield?
options: A) Oxygenation and downstream recovery are irrelevant once the gene is present
B) P has an upstream growth limitation, while Q has a downstream recovery limitation; expression is only one factor in final yield
C) Q must have lost every transgene because purification losses are DNA mutations
D) P and Q must have equal product yield because per-cell expression was once equal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Upstream culture performance and downstream recovery can independently limit final yield.
Why: Product accumulated in a bioreactor depends on viable producing biomass and sustained physiological conditions, including adequate oxygenation for the stated culture. P's scale-up problem reduces that production capacity. Q instead loses material after production during processing, separation or purification. A per-cell expression measurement made in a small flask therefore omits both the number of productive cells over time and the fraction of their product recovered in usable form.
Why not the others: (A) treats gene presence as sufficient for the entire production process. (C) confuses physical recovery loss with a genetic change. (D) transfers a controlled small-scale measurement to different large-scale and processing conditions.
Key point: Distinguish expression, culture productivity and recoverable purified product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Local hybridisation counts across alkene, alkyne, methylene and aldehyde centres
questions.syllabus_anchor: Chemical Bonding: hybridisation; local molecular structure
questions.question: For CH2=CH–C≡C–CH2–CHO, count only the six carbon atoms and use the usual local hybridisation model. What are the numbers of sp, sp2 and sp3 carbons, respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Two sp, three sp2 and one sp3 carbon.
Step 1: Each of the two alkyne carbons has two electron-domain directions and is sp. Each of the two alkene carbons has three directions and is sp2.
Step 2: The aldehyde carbon also has three directions because its double-bonded oxygen counts as one direction, so it is sp2. The intervening CH2 has four sigma-bond directions and is sp3.
Why: Hybridisation is assigned locally; the presence of several multiple bonds does not make every carbon in the molecule the same type. Conjugation does not change the intervening saturated CH2 into a carbon with three bond directions.
Why not the others: (B) counts the carbonyl carbon as sp3. (C) counts only one of the two alkyne carbons as sp. (D) assigns an extra sp centre despite its three-direction bonding.
Key point: Count electron-domain directions separately at each carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ligand-set exchange between complex cation and anion preserves oxidation states and total composition
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordination Compounds: coordination isomerism; charge balance
questions.question: Compounds P=[Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and Q=[Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6] are considered with NH3 neutral, CN− monodentate and both metals in oxidation state +3. Which relationship and charge accounting are correct?
options: A) Linkage isomers; every complex ion is neutral
B) Coordination isomers; each has a 3+ complex cation and a 3− complex anion
C) Ionisation isomers; CN− changes from monodentate to bidentate
D) Geometrical isomers; one metal must change oxidation state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) They are coordination isomers with complex-ion charges +3 and -3.
Step 1: A six-ammine M(III) ion has charge +3. A six-cyanido M(III) ion has charge \(+3-6=-3\). Both written salts therefore balance electrically.
Step 2: The ligand sets are exchanged between two different metal centres in the complex cation and complex anion while the total composition is retained. This is coordination isomerism.
Why: Classifying the isomerism requires identifying what changes: the distribution of ligands between complex ions, rather than the donor atom of one ambidentate ligand or spatial arrangement within a fixed complex.
Why not the others: (A) invents a changed donor atom and miscounts ionic charges. (C) invokes a simple counterion exchange and a denticity change that do not occur. (D) changes neither metal's stated oxidation state and misidentifies the structural rearrangement.
Key point: Establish ionic composition before naming a coordination-isomer relationship.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: An interior radial node and shell-volume factor distinguish 2s density from radial probability
questions.syllabus_anchor: Structure of Atom: quantum mechanical model; orbital shapes; radial and angular nodes
questions.question: The angular probability distribution of an orbital is spherical. Its radial probability P(r) is graphed: it vanishes at r=0 and at one positive radius, but is positive on both sides of that interior zero. Also P(r)/r2 approaches a positive constant at the origin. Use P(r) proportional to r2 times the local probability density, angular-node count l and radial-node count n-l-1. Which orbital and nuclear-position density follow?
options: A) 1s; the density must be zero because P(0)=0
B) 2p; spherical angular probability requires l=1
C) 2s; the local density at the nucleus is nonzero despite P(0)=0
D) 3s; every zero including the radial origin counts as a radial node
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It is 2s, and the local probability density at the nucleus is nonzero.
Step 1: Spherical angular distribution identifies an s orbital, with l=0 and no angular nodes.
Step 2: The graph has one node at a positive radius. The radial origin is a boundary, not an additional nodal shell. Thus \(n-l-1=1\) gives n=2.
Step 3: The given relation means local density is proportional to P(r)/r². Its specified positive limit therefore gives nonzero density at the nucleus.
Why: Radial probability includes the size of a spherical shell. That geometrical factor vanishes at zero radius even when the local density does not. The graph must be interpreted as the stated radial quantity, not as the wavefunction itself.
Why not the others: (A) omits the interior node and confuses the two probability quantities. (B) contradicts the spherical angular distribution. (D) counts a boundary as an extra radial node.
Key point: Distinguish radial probability, local density and an interior nodal shell.
questions.image_alt: Radial probability has two positive lobes separated by a node at 2a0; the origin is also zero from the shell factor.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Two-step profile distinguishes local activation height from an absolute peak ordinate
questions.syllabus_anchor: Organic Chemistry—Basic Principles: reaction intermediates; energy profile
questions.question: The two-step reaction profile has reactants at 0, first transition state at +40, intermediate at -40, second transition state at +30 and products at -20 kJ mol−1. What are the larger local forward activation barrier and the overall reaction enthalpy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The larger local barrier is 70 kJ mol⁻¹ and the overall enthalpy is -20 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: Each activation barrier is measured from the minimum immediately preceding its transition state.
Formula/Principle: Local barrier is transition-state energy minus its starting-state energy; overall enthalpy is final minus initial energy in this supplied profile.
Step 1: First-step barrier is \(40-0=40\) kJ mol⁻¹. Second-step barrier is \[30-(-40)=70\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.\]
Step 2: Overall change is \[-20-0=-20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.\]
Why: The lower absolute second peak still rises farther above its own deeper intermediate. Comparing peak heights alone does not compare local activation energies. This calculation does not by itself assert an overall rate-limiting step without population assumptions.
Why not the others: (A) reports the first barrier. (B) uses an absolute peak ordinate as a barrier. (C) reverses the sign of the reactant-to-product change.
Key point: Measure each barrier from its own preceding minimum.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Fused aromatic vertex counting separated from a single localised-bond picture
questions.syllabus_anchor: Hydrocarbons: aromatic hydrocarbons; resonance; fused rings
questions.question: The figure shows a fused two-hexagon aromatic hydrocarbon with one shared edge; every unlabelled vertex is carbon and only the required hydrogens are omitted. What formula and interpretation of the alternating-bond drawing are correct?
options: A) C12H12; the rings are separate cyclohexanes
B) C10H8; the drawing is one resonance contributor, not proof of permanently localised alternating bonds
C) C12H10; the rings share no carbon atoms
D) C10H10; every carbon has one hydrogen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The fused aromatic structure is C10H8 and is described by resonance.
Step 1: Two six-carbon rings share the two carbons on their common edge, giving \(6+6-2=10\) carbon atoms.
Step 2: The two shared junction carbons already bond to three other carbons and have no hydrogen. The remaining eight peripheral carbons each carry one hydrogen.
Why: A Kekulé-style alternating-bond sketch is a way of representing a conjugated aromatic system; it is not evidence that one fixed set of separate double bonds fully describes its electronic structure. Counting shared vertices also distinguishes fused rings from two rings linked by a single bond.
Why not the others: (A) ignores both fusion and unsaturation. (C) counts the two shared carbons twice and describes a different topology. (D) assigns hydrogens to the ring-junction carbons despite their valence.
Key point: Count the fused graph before adding hydrogens.
questions.image_alt: Two fused hexagons share two junction carbons and one edge; only one resonance contributor is drawn.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Halogen deactivation and ortho/para direction describe different kinetic comparisons
questions.syllabus_anchor: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes: electrophilic substitution of haloarenes
questions.question: Chlorobenzene undergoes electrophilic nitration more slowly than benzene under comparable conditions, yet its principal substitution positions are ortho and para. Which explanation reconciles rate and orientation?
options: A) Chlorine's inductive withdrawal can deactivate the ring while lone-pair resonance influences the relative stability of ortho/para attack pathways
B) Every electron-withdrawing substituent must direct exclusively meta, so the observations are impossible
C) A slower rate proves that chlorine cannot donate any electron density by resonance
D) Ortho/para direction proves that chlorobenzene must react faster than benzene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Overall reactivity and relative positional preference need not have the same trend.
Why: The halogen's electron-withdrawing inductive effect lowers the ring's overall susceptibility to electrophilic substitution. Its lone-pair interaction can nevertheless influence the relative stabilisation of intermediates for attack at different positions, favouring ortho and para relative to meta. Deactivation compares the substituted ring with benzene, whereas orientation compares competing positions within that substituted ring. These are different comparisons, so the stated combination is consistent.
Why not the others: (B) applies an exceptionless rule that fails for halogens. (C) treats one net kinetic observation as proof that a competing electronic effect is absent. (D) equates positional direction with overall activation.
Key point: Keep the reference comparison for rate distinct from the comparison among substitution sites.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: A Williamson target has one suitable reagent orientation and one invalid aryl-SN2 reversal
questions.syllabus_anchor: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers: preparation of ethers; Williamson synthesis
questions.question: Two Williamson routes are proposed for phenetole, Ph–O–CH2CH3, under ordinary SN2 conditions: P uses sodium phenoxide and bromoethane; Q uses sodium ethoxide and bromobenzene. Which assessment is correct?
options: A) Both routes are equivalent because their total atom counts match
B) Only Q is suitable because an aryl carbon is the easier SN2 centre
C) P is suitable; Q incorrectly treats the aryl C–Br centre as an ordinary SN2 substrate
D) Neither route can form an ether because alkoxides never act as nucleophiles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Phenoxide attacks the primary alkyl halide in P; Q is not the equivalent reversed route.
Why: Williamson synthesis requires a suitable substitution centre. Bromoethane offers a primary sp3 carbon at which phenoxide can displace bromide. Reversing the partners leaves bromine on an aromatic sp2 carbon; ordinary backside SN2 substitution at that aryl centre is not the corresponding viable process. Atom balance is necessary for a synthetic proposal but does not establish the required mechanism.
Why not the others: (A) ignores which atom bears the leaving group. (B) reverses the usual substrate suitability. (D) denies the nucleophilic role of alkoxide or phenoxide oxygen.
Key point: Choose which side supplies the nucleophile and which supplies the substitutable alkyl carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Carbonyl-carbon isotope retention resolves an otherwise ambiguous oxidative acid-fragment pair
questions.syllabus_anchor: Aldehydes and Ketones: oxidative cleavage; carbon-skeleton accounting
questions.question: Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one are candidates for an unknown ketone. Under the specified oxidative-cleavage conditions both candidates can give one ethanoic-acid and one propanoic-acid fragment. The original carbonyl carbon is 13C-labelled, remains in one acid's carboxyl group, and no carbon scrambling occurs. The label is found in ethanoic acid. Which inference follows?
options: A) Only pentan-3-one fits because its carbonyl carbon has a methyl neighbour
B) Neither candidate can contain five carbon atoms
C) The unlabelled product pair already uniquely identifies pentan-2-one
D) Pentan-2-one fits; pentan-3-one would retain its carbonyl carbon with an ethyl group in labelled propanoic acid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The isotope location, rather than the unlabelled acid pair alone, selects pentan-2-one.
Step 1: Pentan-2-one has a carbonyl carbon next to methyl and propyl groups. In the specified two-plus-three-carbon cleavage, retention with methyl gives labelled ethanoic acid.
Step 2: Pentan-3-one has an ethyl group on each side of its carbonyl. Retaining either side with that carbon gives a three-carbon labelled acid, propanoic acid.
Why: The supplied label tracks the original carbonyl carbon through a carbon-conserving cleavage. Without that tracking, the same pair of unlabelled fragment formulas would not distinguish the candidates under the stated conditions. No universal regioselectivity beyond the supplied cleavage model is assumed.
Why not the others: (A) gives pentan-3-one a methyl neighbour it does not possess. (B) ignores the conserved total of two plus three carbons. (C) discards the stated ambiguity that the isotope experiment resolves.
Key point: Track atom identity when product formulas alone are ambiguous.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: A temporary amino directing group establishes an alternating bromine pattern before reductive removal
questions.syllabus_anchor: Amines: diazotisation; replacement of diazonium group by hydrogen
questions.question: Aniline is brominated with excess bromine water to give the usual 2,4,6-tribromo derivative. Its amino group is then diazotised at 0–5 degrees C and replaced by hydrogen using H3PO2, with the bromines retained. Which final aromatic product is obtained after renumbering the ring?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1,3,5-Tribromobenzene.
Step 1: The amino group activates the original ortho and para positions, giving bromines at positions 2,4,6 relative to the original NH2 carbon.
Step 2: Cold diazotisation converts NH2 to the diazonium group. H3PO2 replaces that group by H rather than by OH or CN. The three bromine positions are unchanged.
Step 3: Without the original amino substituent, renumbering from a brominated carbon gives the alternating pattern 1,3,5.
Why: A temporary directing group can establish a substitution pattern and then be removed; replacing the group does not move the other substituents.
Why not the others: (B) stops before diazotisation and deamination. (C) uses the hydrolysis product associated with water rather than the supplied reducing reagent. (D) removes two bromines without a stipulated reaction.
Key point: Preserve ring connectivity while renumbering after removal of a directing group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: A second nonvolatile solute changes the full solvent mole-fraction denominator
questions.syllabus_anchor: Solutions: Raoult's law; vapour-pressure lowering
questions.question: One mole of solvent is mixed ideally with 0.10 mol nonvolatile solute X and 0.15 mol nonvolatile solute Y. Neither associates nor dissociates. What is the final solvent vapour pressure divided by its pure vapour pressure, and why is it not 1/1.10?
options: A) 0.90; only X can affect vapour pressure
B) 0.80; both solutes enter the total mole count
C) 0.75; mole fraction equals one minus total solute moles
D) 1.25; adding solute increases solvent mole fraction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The ratio is 0.80 because both nonvolatile solutes contribute particles.
Given: Solvent amount is 1.00 mol and total solute amount is 0.25 mol.
Formula/Principle: For an ideal solution with nonvolatile solutes, \(p_{solvent}=x_{solvent}p^0\).
Step 1: \[x_{solvent}=1.00/(1.00+0.10+0.15)=1/1.25=0.80.\]
Step 2: The ratio 1/1.10 would omit Y from the denominator even though it is another dissolved particle population.
Why: Raoult's law uses mole fraction in the entire liquid mixture, not a separately normalised solvent–X subsystem.
Why not the others: (A) neglects Y and also approximates the remaining ratio incorrectly. (C) subtracts amounts without dividing by total moles. (D) inverts the mole-fraction ratio.
Key point: Include every dissolved species in the mole-fraction denominator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Electron-weighted Gibbs-energy addition combines unequal-electron reduction steps
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electrochemistry: electrode potentials; Gibbs energy and cell emf
questions.question: Standard reduction potentials are A3+ + e− → A2+, E1°=+0.50 V, and A2+ + 2e− → A(s), E2°=-0.10 V. What is E° for A3+ + 3e− → A(s), and its standard Gibbs energy change expressed using Faraday constant F?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The combined potential is +0.10 V and ΔG°=-0.30F.
Given: The two reductions have different electron counts and sum to the target reaction.
Formula/Principle: Gibbs energies are additive; potentials themselves are not extensive.
Step 1: \[\Delta G_1^\circ=-F(0.50),\quad\Delta G_2^\circ=-2F(-0.10)=+0.20F.\]
Step 2: \[\Delta G_{sum}^\circ=-0.30F.\]
Step 3: The total electron count is three, so \[E^\circ=-\Delta G_{sum}^\circ/(3F)=0.10\ \mathrm V.\]
Why: Electron weighting enters through the energy relation before converting back to the intensive potential.
Why not the others: (A) directly adds potentials. (B) takes an unweighted arithmetic mean. (D) reverses the sign of the final reduction.
Key point: Add energies for combined electrochemical reactions, then divide by the total electron count.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Excess-reactant control changes the observed order and slope without changing the intrinsic law
questions.syllabus_anchor: Chemical Kinetics: rate law; pseudo-first-order reactions
questions.question: A reaction has intrinsic rate law r=k[A][B]. In two runs B is maintained in large excess so its concentration changes negligibly. Run P uses [B]=0.20 M and run Q uses [B]=0.40 M. What logarithmic A-time behaviour and interpretation follow?
options: A) Neither run can have a straight ln[A] plot because the intrinsic overall order is two
B) Both show straight ln[A] plots with equal slope because the same temperature fixes k
C) Q must be zero order because it contains more B
D) Both can show apparent first-order A decay, with Q's slope magnitude twice P's, while intrinsic overall order remains two
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Excess B produces a pseudo-first-order observation without changing the intrinsic two-reactant law.
Step 1: With B effectively constant in each run, \[r=(k[B]) [A]=k_{obs}[A].\]
Step 2: Integration gives \(\ln[A]=\ln[A]_0-k_{obs}t\). Thus ln[A] is linear in time.
Step 3: \[k_{obs,Q}/k_{obs,P}=0.40/0.20=2.\]
Why: The controlled concentration becomes part of the observed coefficient. A first-order trace in one monitored reactant is not proof that the intrinsic law contains only that reactant.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the excess-reactant approximation. (B) confuses constant intrinsic k with the concentration-dependent observed coefficient. (C) assigns an order from amount alone.
Key point: Distinguish an intrinsic rate constant from a pseudo-order coefficient.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: A matched dilution blank changes the inferred weak-acid ionisation enthalpy
questions.syllabus_anchor: Thermodynamics: calorimetry; Hess's law; enthalpy of ionisation
questions.question: At the same temperature, neutralising 0.100 mol strong acid with strong base releases 5.70 kJ. Neutralising 0.100 mol weak monoprotic acid HA with the same base releases 5.20 kJ as measured. A matched dilution blank for the weak-acid run releases 0.20 kJ and is included in that measured heat. What molar enthalpy of HA ionisation follows? Assume the remaining reaction steps are identical.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) HA ionisation is endothermic by 7.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: Positive quoted heats mean energy released; the blank is a nonreaction contribution.
Formula/Principle: Hess's law compares the weak-acid reaction with the strong-ion neutralisation after subtracting the blank.
Step 1: Weak-acid reaction heat release alone is \(5.20-0.20=5.00\) kJ. Its molar reaction enthalpy is -50.0 kJ mol⁻¹; the strong-acid value is -57.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Dissociation followed by proton neutralisation gives the weak-acid reaction. \[\Delta H_{ion}+(-57.0)=-50.0\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta H_{ion}=+7.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.\]
Why: Ionisation absorbs some of the heat released in the common proton–hydroxide step. A dilution background must not be assigned to that ionisation.
Why not the others: (B) omits the dilution correction. (C) reverses the enthalpy sign. (D) fails to convert the 0.100 mol heat difference to a per-mole value.
Key point: Correct measured heat contributions before using a Hess comparison.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Solid-phase exhaustion limits equilibrium gas pressure in one of two otherwise identical vessels
questions.syllabus_anchor: Equilibrium: heterogeneous equilibria; reaction quotient; material balance
questions.question: For CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s)+CO2(g), Kp=0.40 bar at a fixed temperature. Two identical rigid vessels have RT/V=1.00 bar mol−1 and initially contain no CO2 but 0.50 mol CaO. P contains 1.00 mol CaCO3; Q contains only 0.10 mol CaCO3. What are the final CO2 pressures, allowing a solid phase to be exhausted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P reaches 0.40 bar while Q exhausts carbonate at 0.10 bar.
Given: Each mole CO2 raises pressure by 1.00 bar in either vessel.
Formula/Principle: The Kp pressure condition for the displayed heterogeneous equilibrium requires both solid phases to remain available.
Step 1: Reaching 0.40 bar requires decomposition of 0.40 mol carbonate. P has enough, leaving 0.60 mol and retaining both solids.
Step 2: Q can release only 0.10 mol CO2 before its carbonate disappears. \[p_Q=(0.10\ \mathrm{mol})(1.00\ \mathrm{bar\,mol^{-1}})=0.10\ \mathrm{bar}.\]
Why: Once a required solid phase is absent, blindly setting the gas pressure to Kp would demand more reactant than exists. The phase-exhausted boundary must satisfy the material inventory.
Why not the others: (A) ignores Q's limiting carbonate amount. (C) equates all P carbonate with obligatory decomposition despite equilibrium. (D) reverses the inventories.
Key point: Check phase availability before imposing a heterogeneous equilibrium expression.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Formal f-electron accounting linked to lanthanoid exceptions and actinoid oxidation-state variation
questions.syllabus_anchor: The d- and f-Block Elements: lanthanoids; actinoids; oxidation states
questions.question: Use the neutral configurations Ce: [Xe]4f1 5d1 6s2, Eu: [Xe]4f7 6s2 and U: [Rn]5f3 6d1 7s2. In the usual formal valence-electron accounting for Ce4+, Eu2+ and U6+, which f counts and interpretation are consistent?
options: A) Ce 4f1, Eu 4f5, U 5f3; oxidation removes only s electrons forever
B) Ce 4f0, Eu 4f7, U 5f0; these states arise because atomic mass alone fixes oxidation number
C) Ce 4f0, Eu 4f7, U 5f0; empty or half-filled arrangements can matter, and nearby actinoid valence-orbital energies permit wider oxidation-state variation
D) Ce 4f4, Eu 4f9, U 5f6; positive charge adds f electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The formal counts are 4f0, 4f7 and 5f0, with electron energetics rather than atomic mass as the relevant explanation.
Step 1: Ce loses its two 6s, one 5d and one 4f valence electrons to reach Ce4+, leaving 4f0.
Step 2: Eu loses its two 6s electrons to form Eu2+, preserving the half-filled 4f7 arrangement.
Step 3: U6+ formally loses the six electrons distributed over 7s,6d and5f, leaving 5f0.
Why: The dominant +3 tendency of lanthanoids does not prohibit particular +2 or +4 states. Empty or half-filled configurations contribute to some exceptions, while participation of nearby-energy actinoid orbitals allows a wider range of oxidation states. This is not a prediction that every formally writable ion is equally stable in every medium.
Why not the others: (A) stops removing electrons despite the required charges. (B) has the counts but replaces orbital energetics with an unsupported mass rule. (D) gives cations extra electrons instead of removing them.
Key point: Reconcile charge with the whole valence configuration before explaining f-block exceptions.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Concrete matrix identity reduces a high-degree polynomial to a linear matrix expression
questions.syllabus_anchor: Matrices and Determinants: matrix multiplication; polynomial identities; determinants
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}\), which satisfies A²-3A+2I=0. Find \(\det(A^5-3A^4+4A^2-I)\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) -1.
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix},\quad A^2-3A+2I=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(A^2=3A-2I\ \text{reduces every higher power}\)
Step 1: \(A^3=3A^2-2A=3(3A-2I)-2A=7A-6I\)
Step 2: \(A^5-3A^4=A^3(A^2-3A)=A^3(-2I)=-2A^3=-14A+12I\)
Step 3: \(4A^2=12A-8I\)
Step 4: \(A^5-3A^4+4A^2-I=(-14A+12I)+(12A-8I)-I=3I-2A\)
Worked derivation: \[3I-2A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\4&-3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=(3)(-3)-(-2)(4)=-9+8=-1\]
Check: \[\lambda=1,2;\ p(\lambda)=\lambda^5-3\lambda^4+4\lambda^2-1:\ p(1)=1,\ p(2)=32-48+16-1=-1;\quad\det=p(1)p(2)=-1\]
Why: \(\text{polynomials in the same matrix commute and reduce like ordinary polynomials}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+1\ (\text{sign lost})\); (C) \(3\ (\text{one diagonal entry})\); (D) \(-3\ (\text{one diagonal entry})\).
Key point: \(\det p(A)=\prod p(\lambda_i)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Repeated intact blocks and disjoint endpoint cases in a multiset arrangement
questions.syllabus_anchor: Permutations and Combinations: repeated objects; restrictions
questions.question: Five tiles consist of two identical tiles marked AB, two identical tiles marked C and one tile marked D. Tiles remain intact in a row. How many distinct rows have D at either end?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 12.
Given: \(\text{tiles}:\ AB,\ AB,\ C,\ C,\ D;\quad D\ \text{at an end}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{arrangements with repeats}=\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}\)
Step 1: \(D\ \text{at the left end}:\ \dfrac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6\)
Step 2: \(D\ \text{at the right end}:\ \dfrac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6\)
Worked derivation: \[N=6+6=12\]
Check: \[\text{all rows}:\ \frac{5!}{2!\,2!}=30;\quad P(D\ \text{at an end})=\frac25;\quad30\times\frac25=12\]
Why: \(\text{there is one}\ D,\ \text{so the two cases cannot overlap}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(6\ (\text{one end only})\); (B) \(24=2\times\tfrac{4!}{2!}\); (C) \(30\ (D\ \text{anywhere})\).
Key point: \(\text{divide by the factorial of each group of identical tiles}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: An onto composition constrains the final factor but leaves an unused intermediate element
questions.syllabus_anchor: Relations and Functions: composition; onto functions; finite maps
questions.question: Let f:{1,2,3}→{a,b,c,d} map 1,2,3 to a,b,c respectively. How many maps g:{a,b,c,d}→{0,1} make g∘f onto {0,1}, and what does this require of f and g?
options: A) 12; g must be onto, while f need not be onto its stated codomain
B) 12; f must be onto, while g need not be onto
C) 14; both factors must be onto
D) 6; neither factor can be onto
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 12; g must be onto, while f need not be onto its stated codomain.
Given: \(f:1\mapsto a,\ 2\mapsto b,\ 3\mapsto c;\quad g:\{a,b,c,d\}\to\{0,1\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(g\circ f\ \text{onto}\iff g(\{a,b,c\})=\{0,1\}\)
Step 1: \(\text{assignments of}\ g\ \text{on}\ \{a,b,c\}:\ 2^3=8\)
Step 2: \(\text{constant ones}:\ 2\Rightarrow8-2=6\)
Step 3: \(g(d)\in\{0,1\}:\ 2\ \text{choices}\)
Worked derivation: \[N=(2^3-2)\times2=12\]
Check: \[\text{all}\ g:\ 2^4=16;\quad g\ \text{constant on}\ \{a,b,c\}:\ 2\times2=4;\quad16-4=12\]
Why: \(g(\{a,b,c\})=\{0,1\}\Rightarrow g\ \text{onto};\quad d\notin f(\{1,2,3\})\Rightarrow f\ \text{not onto}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f\ \text{misses}\ d\); (C) \(14=2^4-2\ (\text{counts onto}\ g,\ \text{not onto}\ g\circ f)\); (D) \(6\ (\text{omits the choice of}\ g(d))\).
Key point: \(g\circ f\ \text{onto}\Rightarrow g\ \text{onto}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Conjugate pairing and cubic root product determine a real but negative square sum
questions.syllabus_anchor: Complex Numbers: conjugates; Quadratic and Polynomial Equations: roots and coefficients
questions.question: A real-coefficient cubic is x³+ax²+bx-10 and has root 1+2i. What is the sum of the squares of all three roots, counting multiplicity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) -2.
Given: \(x^3+ax^2+bx-10=0\ (a,b\in\mathbb R),\quad r_1=1+2i\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_2=\bar r_1;\quad r_1r_2r_3=-\dfrac{(-10)}1=10\)
Step 1: \(r_2=1-2i,\quad r_1r_2=1+4=5\)
Step 2: \(r_3=\dfrac{10}5=2\)
Step 3: \(r_1^2=1+4i-4=-3+4i,\quad r_2^2=-3-4i,\quad r_3^2=4\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum r_j^2=(-3+4i)+(-3-4i)+4=-2\]
Check: \[\sum r_j=4,\ \sum r_ir_j=5+2(2)=9:\quad\left(\sum r_j\right)^2-2\sum r_ir_j=16-18=-2\]
Why: \(\text{squares of complex roots are not squared moduli}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+2\ (\text{sign lost})\); (B) \(10=r_1r_2r_3\); (D) \(14=|r_1|^2+|r_2|^2+r_3^2=5+5+4\).
Key point: \(\sum r_j^2=\left(\sum r_j\right)^2-2\sum r_ir_j\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A minimum of two curves and an absolute value require two different sets of breakpoints
questions.syllabus_anchor: Integral Calculus: piecewise definite integrals; areas
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left|\min\{x^2,2-x^2\}\right|\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 16(√2-1)/3.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^2\left|\min\{x^2,2-x^2\}\right|dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{even integrand}\Rightarrow I=2\displaystyle\int_0^2;\quad\text{break at}\ x^2=2-x^2\ \text{and at}\ 2-x^2=0\)
Step 1: \(x^2=2-x^2\Rightarrow x=1;\qquad2-x^2=0\Rightarrow x=\sqrt2\)
Step 2: \([0,1]:\ \min=x^2\ge0;\quad[1,\sqrt2]:\ \min=2-x^2\ge0;\quad[\sqrt2,2]:\ \min=2-x^2\le0\)
Step 3: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1x^2dx=\tfrac13\)
Step 4: \(\displaystyle\int_1^{\sqrt2}(2-x^2)dx=\left[2x-\tfrac{x^3}3\right]_1^{\sqrt2}=\tfrac{4\sqrt2}3-\tfrac53\)
Step 5: \(\displaystyle\int_{\sqrt2}^2(x^2-2)dx=\left[\tfrac{x^3}3-2x\right]_{\sqrt2}^2=-\tfrac43+\tfrac{4\sqrt2}3\)
Worked derivation: \[I=2\left(\tfrac13-\tfrac53-\tfrac43+\tfrac{8\sqrt2}3\right)=\frac{16(\sqrt2-1)}3\approx2.21\]
Check: \[\tfrac13\approx0.333,\ \tfrac{4\sqrt2-5}3\approx0.219,\ \tfrac{4\sqrt2-4}3\approx0.552:\quad2(1.105)\approx2.21\]
Why: \(\text{the switch of the minimum (at 1) and its sign change (at}\ \sqrt2)\ \text{are different points}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0\ (\text{signed integral})\); (B) \(\tfrac{8(\sqrt2-1)}3\ (\text{half-range only})\); (C) \(\tfrac{16\sqrt2}3\ (\text{constants dropped})\).
Key point: \(\text{find every breakpoint before removing}\ |\cdot|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A direction parameter gives parallelism while an independent base-point parameter gives coincidence
questions.syllabus_anchor: Three-dimensional Geometry: vector equations of lines; parallel and coincident lines
questions.question: Lines L1=(1,0,2)+t(1,2,-1) and L2=(b,2,1)+s(2,k,-2) depend on real b,k. Which pair makes them the same line, rather than merely parallel?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) k=4,b=2.
Given: \(L_1:(1,0,2)+t(1,2,-1),\quad L_2:(b,2,1)+s(2,k,-2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{same line}\iff\vec d_2\parallel\vec d_1\ \text{and}\ P_2-P_1\parallel\vec d_1\)
Step 1: \((2,k,-2)=\mu(1,2,-1)\Rightarrow\mu=2,\ k=4\)
Step 2: \(P_2-P_1=(b-1,\ 2,\ -1)=\lambda(1,2,-1)\)
Step 3: \(2=2\lambda,\ -1=-\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=1\Rightarrow b-1=1\Rightarrow b=2\)
Worked derivation: \[k=4,\quad b=2:\qquad(2,2,1)=(1,0,2)+1\cdot(1,2,-1)\]
Check: \[b=4:\ (3,2,-1)\ne\lambda(1,2,-1)\Rightarrow\text{parallel, distinct}\]
Why: \(\text{parallel directions alone allow two distinct lines}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(b=4:\ \text{parallel but distinct}\); (C) \(k=2:\ (2,2,-2)\nparallel(1,2,-1)\); (D) \(k=-4:\ (2,-4,-2)\nparallel(1,2,-1)\).
Key point: \(\text{coincident lines share a direction and a point}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: An indeterminate implicit derivative is resolved through two explicit branches with a shared tangent
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differentiation: implicit functions; tangent interpretation
questions.question: For the real curve y²=x⁴, the formula y'=2x³/y gives 0/0 at the origin. What are the tangent lines there when both real branches are considered?
options: A) Both branches have the horizontal tangent y=0
B) Both branches have the vertical tangent x=0
C) The two branches have slopes +1 and -1
D) No real branch passes through the origin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both branches have the horizontal tangent y=0.
Given: \(y^2=x^4\)
Formula/Principle: \(y^2-x^4=(y-x^2)(y+x^2)=0\)
Step 1: \(y=x^2\ \ \text{or}\ \ y=-x^2\)
Step 2: \(y'=2x\ \ \text{or}\ \ y'=-2x\)
Step 3: \(x=0:\ y'=0\ \text{on both branches}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{both branches pass through}\ (0,0)\ \text{with slope}\ 0\Rightarrow\text{tangent}\ y=0\]
Check: \[y=x^2:\ \frac{2x^3}y=\frac{2x^3}{x^2}=2x\to0\ \ (x\to0)\]
Why: \(\tfrac00\ \text{in}\ y'=\tfrac{2x^3}y\ \text{is indeterminate, not infinite}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(y'=0,\ \text{not}\ \infty\); (C) \(y'(0)=0\ne\pm1\); (D) \(0^2=0^4\).
Key point: \(\text{factor the curve into branches at a singular point}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Pairing observations with affine reflections changes a pooled variance through mean separation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Statistics: mean; population variance; affine changes
questions.question: A data set has n observations, mean 2 and population variance 3. A new set of 2n observations contains every original x once and its reflected value 8-x once. What are the new mean and population variance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 and 7.
Given: \(\bar x=2,\quad\sigma^2=3;\quad\text{new set}:\ x_i\ \text{and}\ 8-x_i\ \ (2n\ \text{values})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sigma_{\text{new}}^2=\dfrac1{2n}\sum\left[(x_i-\mu)^2+(8-x_i-\mu)^2\right]\)
Step 1: \(\mu=\dfrac1{2n}\sum\left[x_i+(8-x_i)\right]=\dfrac{8n}{2n}=4\)
Step 2: \(8-x_i-4=-(x_i-4)\Rightarrow\sigma_{\text{new}}^2=\dfrac1n\sum(x_i-4)^2\)
Step 3: \((x_i-4)^2=(x_i-2)^2-4(x_i-2)+4\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma_{\text{new}}^2=3-4(0)+4=7,\qquad\mu=4\]
Check: \[\text{groups with means}\ 2,\ 6\ \text{and variance}\ 3:\quad3+\frac{(2-4)^2+(6-4)^2}2=3+4=7\]
Why: \(\text{reflection keeps each group's variance but separates the group means}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3\ (\text{between-group term omitted})\); (B) \(\mu=2\ (\text{mean of the original only})\); (D) \(\mu=6\ (\text{mean of the reflected only})\).
Key point: \(\text{total variance}=\text{within-group}+\text{between-group}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A floor-function squeeze controls a trigonometric quotient at infinity
questions.syllabus_anchor: Limits and Continuity: standard limits; inequalities; functions
questions.question: Let ⌊x⌋ be the greatest integer not exceeding x. Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}x\sin\frac1{\lfloor x\rfloor}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.
Given: \(L=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}x\sin\frac1{\lfloor x\rfloor}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n=\lfloor x\rfloor:\ n\le x<n+1;\quad\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}u=1\)
Step 1: \(1\le\dfrac xn<1+\dfrac1n\Rightarrow\dfrac xn\to1\)
Step 2: \(x\sin\dfrac1n=\dfrac xn\cdot\dfrac{\sin(1/n)}{1/n}\)
Worked derivation: \[L=1\times1=1\]
Check: \[x=100.5:\ 100.5\sin(0.01)=100.5\times0.0099998\approx1.005\]
Why: \(\text{the jump of}\ \lfloor x\rfloor\ \text{is}\ 1,\ \text{negligible relative to}\ x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0\ (\text{factor}\ x\ \text{ignored})\); (B) \(\text{the squeeze}\ 1\le\tfrac xn<1+\tfrac1n\ \text{gives a limit}\); (C) \(\tfrac xn\to1,\ \text{not}\ 2\).
Key point: \(\dfrac x{\lfloor x\rfloor}\to1\ \text{as}\ x\to\infty\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Different sampling protocols produce different conditional box probabilities from identical contents
questions.syllabus_anchor: Probability: Bayes's theorem; conditional probability; sampling bias
questions.question: Box A contains one red and one blue ball; box B contains three red and one blue. In protocol P, choose a box with probability 1/2 each and then choose a ball uniformly from it. In protocol Q, choose uniformly from all six balls while retaining each ball's box label. Given a red ball, what are P(B|red) in protocols P and Q, respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3/5 and 3/4.
Given: \(A:\ 1R,1B;\quad B:\ 3R,1B\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(B\mid R)=\dfrac{P(B)P(R\mid B)}{P(A)P(R\mid A)+P(B)P(R\mid B)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{P}:\ P(A)=P(B)=\tfrac12,\ P(R\mid A)=\tfrac12,\ P(R\mid B)=\tfrac34\)
Step 2: \(P_P(B\mid R)=\dfrac{\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34}{\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34}=\dfrac{3/8}{5/8}=\dfrac35\)
Step 3: \(\text{Q}:\ 4\ \text{red balls equally likely},\ 3\ \text{from}\ B\)
Worked derivation: \[P_P(B\mid R)=\tfrac35,\qquad P_Q(B\mid R)=\tfrac34\]
Check: \[\text{Q by Bayes}:\ P(B)=\tfrac46,\ P(A)=\tfrac26:\ \frac{\tfrac46\cdot\tfrac34}{\tfrac26\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac46\cdot\tfrac34}=\frac{1/2}{2/3}=\frac34\]
Why: \(\text{choosing a box uniformly is not choosing a ball uniformly when box sizes differ}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{protocols interchanged}\); (C) \(\tfrac12\ (\text{no updating})\); (D) \(P_Q=\tfrac34\ne\tfrac12\).
Key point: \(\text{the prior comes from the sampling mechanism}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A squared trigonometric factor splits connected solution bands without changing sign
questions.syllabus_anchor: Trigonometric Functions: identities; inequalities; periodicity
questions.question: For 0≤x≤5π/2, consider sin(2x)cos x>0. How many connected solution intervals are there, and what is their total length?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Three intervals; 3π/2.
Given: \(\sin2x\cos x>0,\quad0\le x\le\tfrac{5\pi}2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin2x\cos x=2\sin x\cos^2x\)
Step 1: \(2\sin x\cos^2x>0\iff\sin x>0\ \text{and}\ \cos x\ne0\)
Step 2: \(\sin x>0:\ x\in(0,\pi)\cup\left(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}2\right]\)
Step 3: \(\cos x=0:\ x=\tfrac\pi2,\ \tfrac{5\pi}2\ \text{removed}\)
Step 4: \(\left(0,\tfrac\pi2\right),\ \left(\tfrac\pi2,\pi\right),\ \left(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}2\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[N=3,\qquad\text{length}=\tfrac\pi2+\tfrac\pi2+\tfrac\pi2=\tfrac{3\pi}2\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac\pi4:\ 1\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2>0;\quad x=\tfrac{3\pi}4:\ (-1)\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\right)>0;\quad x=\tfrac{5\pi}4:\ (1)\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\right)<0\]
Why: \(\text{removing the single point}\ \tfrac\pi2\ \text{splits an interval without changing the length}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{two intervals ignores the split at}\ \tfrac\pi2\); (C) \(\tfrac{5\pi}2\ \text{is the whole range}\); (D) \(\pi\ \text{omits}\ \left(2\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}2\right)\).
Key point: \(\text{a squared factor removes points but does not change sign}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A singular linear initial-value equation requires a component-specific global minimum
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differential Equations: linear equations; Applications of Derivatives: extrema
questions.question: The solution of \(y'+2y/(x-1)=1/(x-1)^2\), y(0)=1, is taken on its maximal real interval containing zero. What are that interval and the minimum value of y there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (-∞,1); -1/8.
Given: \(y'+\dfrac{2y}{x-1}=\dfrac1{(x-1)^2},\quad y(0)=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int\frac2{x-1}dx}=(x-1)^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac d{dx}\left[(x-1)^2y\right]=1\Rightarrow(x-1)^2y=x+C\)
Step 2: \(y(0)=1:\ 1=C\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x+1}{(x-1)^2}\)
Step 3: \(\text{singular at}\ x=1,\ 0<1\Rightarrow\text{interval}\ (-\infty,1)\)
Step 4: \(y'=\dfrac{(x-1)-2(x+1)}{(x-1)^3}=\dfrac{-(x+3)}{(x-1)^3}\)
Step 5: \(x<-3:\ y'<0;\quad-3<x<1:\ y'>0\)
Worked derivation: \[y_{\min}=y(-3)=\frac{-2}{16}=-\frac18\]
Check: \[x\to-\infty:\ y\to0^-;\quad x\to1^-:\ y\to+\infty;\quad-\tfrac18<0\]
Why: \(\text{a solution cannot be continued through the singular point of the equation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=1\ \text{is excluded}\); (B) \(y(-3)=-\tfrac18<0\); (D) \(0\notin(1,\infty)\).
Key point: \(\text{the solution interval is the component containing the initial point}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Real-root discriminant and strict product positivity yield disconnected parameter intervals
questions.syllabus_anchor: Quadratic Equations: discriminant; roots and coefficients; inequalities
questions.question: For which real a does \(x^2-(a+1)x+2a-1=0\) have real roots, not necessarily distinct, whose product is positive?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (1/2,1]∪[5,∞).
Given: \(x^2-(a+1)x+2a-1=0;\quad\text{real roots},\ \alpha\beta>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta\ge0,\quad\alpha\beta=2a-1\)
Step 1: \(\Delta=(a+1)^2-4(2a-1)=a^2-6a+5=(a-1)(a-5)\)
Step 2: \(\Delta\ge0\Rightarrow a\le1\ \text{or}\ a\ge5\)
Step 3: \(2a-1>0\Rightarrow a>\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[a\in\left(\tfrac12,1\right]\cup[5,\infty)\]
Check: \[a=1:\ x^2-2x+1=0\Rightarrow x=1,1,\ \alpha\beta=1>0;\quad a=3:\ \Delta=-4<0\]
Why: \(\text{equal roots are allowed}\ (\Delta=0);\ \text{zero product is not}\)
Why not the others: (B) \([1,5]:\ \Delta\le0\); (C) \(a=3:\ \Delta<0\); (D) \(a=0:\ \alpha\beta=-1<0\).
Key point: \(\text{intersect the discriminant and Vieta conditions}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: An orthonormal change of coordinates converts a line equation without changing distance
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordinate Geometry: straight lines; distance; orthogonal coordinates
questions.question: Define rotated coordinates u=(3x+4y)/5 and v=(-4x+3y)/5. Which equation describes the line 3x+4y=10 in these coordinates, and what is its perpendicular distance from the origin?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) u=2; distance 2.
Given: \(u=\dfrac{3x+4y}5,\quad v=\dfrac{-4x+3y}5;\quad3x+4y=10\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\ \text{for}\ ax+by=c\)
Step 1: \(3x+4y=5u\Rightarrow5u=10\Rightarrow u=2\)
Step 2: \(d=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{9+16}}=2\)
Worked derivation: \[u=2,\qquad d=2\]
Check: \[\left|\tfrac{(3,4)}5\right|=1,\ \ \tfrac{(3,4)}5\cdot\tfrac{(-4,3)}5=0\Rightarrow\text{rotation}\Rightarrow d=|u|=2\]
Why: \(u\ \text{is the coordinate along the unit normal of the line}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(v=2\ (\text{axes interchanged})\); (B) \(u=10\ (\text{factor 5 omitted})\); (C) \(d=10\ (\text{not normalised})\).
Key point: \(\text{rotations preserve distances}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: An ordered triangle fixes the sign of a plane normal and a signed projection
questions.syllabus_anchor: Vector Algebra: cross and dot products; Three-dimensional Geometry: plane distance
questions.question: A plane is oriented by the ordered points A=(1,0,0), B=(0,1,0), C=(0,0,1), with unit normal along AB×AC. For P=(1,1,1), which normal and signed perpendicular displacement from the plane are correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) n=(1,1,1)/√3; displacement 2/√3.
Given: \(A(1,0,0),\ B(0,1,0),\ C(0,0,1),\ P(1,1,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\hat n=\dfrac{\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}}{|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|},\quad\delta=\vec{AP}\cdot\hat n\)
Step 1: \(\vec{AB}=(-1,1,0),\quad\vec{AC}=(-1,0,1)\)
Step 2: \(\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}=(1\cdot1-0,\ 0\cdot(-1)-(-1)(1),\ 0-(1)(-1))=(1,1,1)\)
Step 3: \(\hat n=\dfrac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt3}\)
Step 4: \(\vec{AP}=(0,1,1)\)
Worked derivation: \[\delta=\frac{0+1+1}{\sqrt3}=\frac2{\sqrt3}\]
Check: \[x+y+z=1:\quad\frac{1+1+1-1}{\sqrt3}=\frac2{\sqrt3}\]
Why: \(\text{the order}\ A,B,C\ \text{fixes the sign of}\ \hat n\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-\tfrac2{\sqrt3}\ (\text{sign inconsistent with}\ \hat n)\); (B) \(\hat n\ \text{reversed gives}\ -\tfrac2{\sqrt3}\); (D) \(|(1,1,1)|=\sqrt3\ne1\).
Key point: \(\text{signed distance}=(\vec P-\vec A)\cdot\hat n\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.sub_topic: A continuous piecewise velocity returns to its start after two reversals but travels a nonzero path
questions.syllabus_anchor: Motion in a Straight Line: velocity-time graph; displacement; distance
questions.question: A particle's velocity graph is v=t-1 m s−1 for 0≤t≤2 s and v=3-t m s−1 for 2≤t≤4 s, with t entered in seconds. What are its displacement and total distance over these four seconds?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Net displacement is zero and distance is 2 m.
Given: Velocity changes sign at t=1 and t=3, not at the continuous join t=2.
Formula/Principle: Displacement is signed area under v(t); distance is area under |v(t)|.
Step 1: Each two-second piece has equal positive and negative triangular areas, giving zero net displacement.
Step 2: There are four triangles of base 1 s and height 1 m s⁻¹.
Worked derivation: \[s=0,\qquad D=4\left(\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot1\right)=2\ \mathrm m.\]
Why: A return to the original position does not erase travelled path. The two direction changes must be used when replacing v by |v|.
Why not the others: (A) treats signed cancellation as zero distance. (C) uses unsigned area for displacement. (D) uses rectangular rather than triangular areas.
Key point: Separate direction reversals from joins between formulas.
